prompt: A team's suite has 40 unit tests and 600 browser-driven end-to-end tests. It takes 70 minutes and fails intermittently. What does the test pyramid suggest?

options.text: Add more end-to-end tests to cover the intermittent failures
options.explanation: That makes the suite slower and flakier. The suite is already inverted (an "ice-cream cone").
A thin layer of end-to-end tests is valuable for checking that the system works as a whole. The pyramid reduces this layer; it doesn't remove it.

options.text: Push most checks down to many fast unit tests and some integration tests, keeping a small set of end-to-end tests for critical journeys
options.explanation: Correct. Lower-level tests are faster, more deterministic and point precisely at the failing code.

options.text: Run the end-to-end tests only once a month
options.explanation: Running them rarely makes their failures harder to trace to a cause. The fix is to have fewer of them and to test most behaviour at lower levels.

workedExample:
1. Current shape: 40 unit, 600 E2E: an inverted pyramid.
2. Cost per test: unit ~ milliseconds, E2E ~ seconds plus browser, network and data setup, which is where flakiness comes from.
3. Illustrative target budget, not measured results: 3,000 unit (about 1 min), 300 integration (about 3 min), 40 E2E tests of critical user journeys (about 6 min).
4. Those assumed durations sum to 10 minutes; benchmark the actual suite and fix sources of nondeterminism rather than assuming a test count guarantees duration or reliability.

link.title: The Practical Test Pyramid — Ham Vocke

prompt: A test suite has 3,600 tests averaging 0.5 s each and runs on one machine. You split the tests evenly across 10 runners, and each runner spends 60 s on setup before testing. Roughly what is the new wall-clock time for the test stage? Assume equal total test duration per test shard, runners starting together, and no queueing or competition for shared resources.

options.explanation: That's 180 s of tests per test shard but forgets each runner's 60 s of setup.
Correct. 3,600 × 0.5 = 1,800 s total; 1,800 / 10 = 180 s per test shard; plus 60 s setup = 240 s = 4 minutes.
That is the original single-machine time (1,800 s). Test sharding runs the test shards in parallel.
This would be total setup across all runners (10 × 60 s), which happens in parallel and isn't additive in wall-clock time.

workedExample:
```formula
t_wall = N × t_test / S + t_setup
t_wall = 3600 × 0.5 s / 10 + 60 s
t_wall = 180 s + 60 s = 240 s = 4 min
C = S × t_wall = 10 × 240 s = 40 min
where
t_wall: the wall-clock time of the test stage, in seconds (s)
N: the number of tests
t_test: the average time per test, in seconds (s)
S: the number of test shards (runners), all starting together
t_setup: each runner's CI setup duration before testing, in seconds (s)
C: the total compute paid for, in runner-minutes
s: seconds
min: minutes; 1 min = 60 s
In words: the tests are divided across the runners, but every runner still pays the full CI setup duration.
```

1. Total test time: 3,600 × 0.5 s = 1,800 s (30 min).
2. Per test shard: 1,800 s / 10 = 180 s.
3. Add each runner's 60 seconds of preparation to its 180 seconds of tests: four elapsed minutes.
4. Total compute is 40 runner-minutes, versus about 31 before, because each of the ten runners repeats preparation. The formula card above shows the calculation.

So test sharding cuts feedback time by nearly 8× (31 min to 4 min) for about 30% more compute. Uneven test shards (one slow test file) can dominate, so balance test shards by measured duration, not count.
